PML-N, PPP headed for one seat each in delayed AJK constituencies. • PPP’s Bazil Ali Naqvi maintains narrow lead in LA-28 • PML-N’s Noreen Arif leads by fewer than 200 votes in LA-27 • Talal tells Bilawal to ‘show grace in defeat’ after PPP cries foul over rigging • AJK speaker alleges 14,000 fake votes after defeat; seeks forensic vote audit in Khawra MUZAFFARABAD / ISLAMABAD: Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) candidates appeared poised to secure one seat each in the two constituencies of Muzaffarabad division where polling was held on Tuesday after being fully or partially deferred on Sunday due to landslides and adverse weather that blocked roads and prevented the timely dispatch of polling staff and election material. According to unofficial and unverified results available past midnight, PPP candidate Syed Bazil Ali Naqvi was maintaining a slender lead over his PML-N rival, Chaudhry Shahzad Mahmood, in LA-28 (Lachhrat). The final consolidation of results was under way when this report went to press. Polling had been held at 122 of the constituency’s 174 polling stations on Sunday. However, after allegations that PPP workers had taken away ballot boxes, the Election Commission ordered repolling at two of those stations, along with polling at the remaining 52 stations where voting could not be held. In LA-27 (Kutla), where polling had been postponed entirely, voting was held at all 197 polling stations on Tuesday. According to unofficial results from all polling stations, PML-N candidate Noreen Arif and Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party (IPP) candidate Sardar Tabarak Ali were separated by fewer than 200 votes, with Ms Arif holding a narrow lead. PML-N leaders expressed confidence that the inclusion of votes cast by government employees on election duty would further consolidate Ms Arif’s lead. Outside her residence, PML-N supporters celebrated by dancing to the beat of drums as counting continued late into the night. Earlier, voting concluded at 5pm amid reports of scuffles and sporadic firing between rival political workers. While both constituencies witnessed allegations of irregularities, the PPP focused most of its criticism on LA-27, whereas the PML-N levelled serious allegations regarding polling in LA-28. In a complaint submitted to the Election Commission, PML-N election cell in-charge Hanif Malik alleged widespread violence, irregularities and voter suppression in LA-28, claiming that armed men resorted to firing and illegally occupied polling stations to inflate votes for the PPP candidate. He alleged that the party’s polling agent at the Nazian polling station in Union Council Panjkot was forcibly expelled, after which polling was conducted unilaterally in favour of the PPP candidate. He further claimed that in Ghorian village of Union Council Muzaffarabad, firing and road blockades prevented PML-N supporters from reaching polling stations. The PPP, on the other hand, alleged that polling staff in LA-27 had been “caught red-handed” with official ballot papers and polling bags inside the house of a PML-N supporter about two kilometres from the designated polling station. The party also circulated a statement by its vice president, Sherry Rehman, in which she described the reports as alarming and said videos purportedly showing “rigging by the PML-N” had been submitted to the Election Commission, urging immediate disciplinary and legal action. Her allegations were repeatedly aired by several television channels. However, Election Commission Senior Member Khawaja Muhammad Ahsan told Dawn that although a PPP worker had submitted videos to the commission, they were “vague and amounted to little more than unverified allegations”. “Unless the footage is authenticated through proper forensic examination and corroborated by other credible evidence, it cannot be treated as proof,” he said. The PPP also shared another complaint addressed to the Election Commission on X, accusing the PML-N of ballot stuffing at polling stations No. 95 and No. 97 in LA-28 and of obstructing the polling process by barring voters from casting their votes. PML-N rejects claims Minister of State for Interior and PML-N’s election coordinator for Poonch division, Tallal Chaudhry, rejected the PPP’s allegations of rigging in the AJK elections and took a swipe at PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, saying “leaders should not cry over defeat”, according to a statement issued by the interior ministry. Presiding over a review meeting on the third phase of the AJK elections in Poonch division, Mr Chaudhry said the PML-N’s sweeping victory in the first two phases reflected public trust in the performance of the federal and Punjab governments. “The people of Kashmir have voted for work and performance,” he told district constituency coordinators and PML-N candidates from Poonch division who attended the meeting. Apparently responding to the PPP’s allegations of electoral malpractices, the minister said: “Bilawal Bhutto should show a big heart. Leaders do not look good when they cry over defeat.” Muzaffarabad Deputy Commissioner Munir Ahmed Qureshi also rejected the PPP’s allegation that polling staff had stayed at the residence of a political figure near the Bheri polling station. Meanwhile, AJK Chief Election Commissioner Justice (retired) Ghulam Mustafa Mughal cast his vote in his native village of Balgran in LA-27. “Voting is a national trust and the responsibility of every citizen,” he said, adding that exercising the right to vote strengthened the democratic system. The first phase of polling was held in AJK’s Mirpur division on July 27, in which the PML-N secured nine of the 13 seats while the PPP won the remaining four. EC rejects postponement rumours Separately, an Election Commission spokesperson dismissed reports that the third phase of elections in Poonch Division had been postponed. “News circulating regarding the postponement of the elections is baseless and contrary to facts,” the spokesperson said, reiterating that polling in all constituencies of Poonch Division would be held on Aug 10 in accordance with the announced schedule. Poonch Division comprises 11 constituencies — three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch and two in Sudhnoti. The spokesperson urged voters to ignore rumours and exercise their right to vote, adding that the commission would promptly inform the public if any change became inevitable. On Monday, Chief Election Commissioner Mughal had said polling would definitely be held in three constituencies of Bagh district, one in Haveli district and one in Abbaspur of Poonch district, while the commission was also considering holding elections in the two Sudhnoti constituencies of Baloch and Palandri if the law and order situation improved. He had said the commission was prepared to conduct polling in all constituencies except Rawalakot city and Thorar, provided voters rejected intimidation and the law and order situation permitted. AJK speaker alleges fake votes Azad Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Latif Akbar on Tuesday accused the Election Commission of failing to ensure free, fair and impartial elections, alleging that more than 14,000 “fake votes” had been cast in favour of his rival in LA-30 Khawra. According to unofficial results, PML-N candidate Raja Saqib Majeed won the seat with 32,511 votes, defeating Mr Akbar by 8,554 votes. Addressing a press conference, the senior PPP leader said he had been in electoral politics for four decades and had won several elections, including during military rule and under opponent governments in Islamabad. “However, I have never witnessed elections as controversial as the ongoing ones in the territory’s history. By no stretch of the imagination can these be called free, fair and impartial,” he alleged. Mr Akbar called for a forensic examination of the votes polled by his rival, saying the PPP was prepared to bear the cost. Published in Dawn, August 5th, 2026

Kara­koram Highway closed, Ghizer worst hit by more flash floods. GILGIT/LAHORE: Flash floods triggered by cloudbursts and rapid glacial melting wreaked hav­oc across Gilgit-Baltis­tan on Tuesday, damaging ho­m­es, roads, bridges and agricultural land, while leaving hundreds of tourists and local residents str­a­nded in several districts. As a result, the Kara­koram Highway (KKH) was closed for traffic near Altashi Nullah in the Gini area of Chilas. Authorities have war­ned that rising water levels in the Hunza, Nagar and Indus rivers, as well as other streams, posed a threat to downstream communities, with riverbank erosion reported in several areas. Heavy rainfall triggered flash floods in various parts of the region, with Ghizer district among the worst affected where an artificial lake was created when flash floods in Mayon village blocked the Ishkoman River. According to local authorities, the artificial lake inundated Hasis village, submerging dozens of houses, agricultural land and public infrastructure. Residents of the affected homes were evacuated after floodwater entered the village. Locals said at least 15 houses were damaged, while a school, a mosque, agricultural fields and other critical infrastructure remained under water. The Ghizer-Ishkoman Road was completely blocked by the artificial lake, severing road access to the Ishkoman Valley, though authorities later said water had started flowing out of the temporary lake. Flash floods also damaged homes and agricultural land in Sherqila, while flooding was reported in Salpi, Aishi, Damas, Haim and Dilnati. Floodwaters also damaged roads and brought down electricity poles at several locations, disrupting power supply. Gilgit-Baltistan Chief Min­i­­ster Amjad Hussain directed the GB Disaster Management Authority and district administrations to expedite rescue, relief and rehabilitation operations. In Gilgit district, cloudburst-indu­ced floods caused widespread damage in the upper reaches of Naltar Valley. According to Rescue 1122 officials, the floods damaged 12 houses, destroyed agricultu­ral land and crops, and displaced several families. The Naltar Highway was blocked at multiple points, leaving tourists stranded. In Upper Hunza, rapid glacial melting damaged sections of the Karakoram Highway near Gulmit. The administration said rising water discharge from Juchar Nallah in the Gojal area temporarily blocked the highway before it was reopened. Jalalpur Pirwala embankments As heavy monsoon rains also cau­s­ed urban flooding in several Punjab cities, provincial minister Khw­aja Salman Rafique visited flood-prone areas and protective embankments in Jalalpur Pirwala to review flood preparedness. Accompanied by PDMA Director General Saif Anwar Jappa, the minister inspected flood embankments, rescue arrangements, evacuation plans and relief preparedness. He said two protective embankments at Jalalpur Pirwala and Nooraja Bhatta had been built at a cost of Rs2 billion, while Rescue 1122 and other departments had been equipped with modern machinery and rescue equipment. He said the government had ensured adequate resources for flood protection. Multan Commissioner Amir Karim briefed the minister that the newly completed 7.2-km embankment at Jalalpur Pirwala would protect the town from backflow in the River Chenab. Digital mapping of flood-prone areas had also been completed, while all departments remained on high alert. According to the PDMA, widespread rainfall was recorded in Punjab, with authorities working to drain accumulated rainwater. The weather system is expected to persist until Wednesday. Hezbollah chief, Lebanese PM trade barbs over talks with Israel. • Qassem says talks will bring Lebanon ‘nothing but shame, humiliation’ • Salam accuses group of ‘helping Israel’ • Talks between both sides continue in Rome BEIRUT: Hezbollah’s chief said on Tuesday that direct talks between Lebanon and Israel would bring only “humiliation” for Lebanon and accused authorities of helping Israel, prompting Lebanon’s prime minister to hit back. The statement came as Lebanon and Israel were preparing to hold a fresh round of direct talks in Rome under US sponsorship, the seventh such meeting since the outbreak of the US-Iran war. “All the direct negotiations will bring Lebanon nothing but shame, humiliation, disappointment and successive concessions,” Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said in a televised address. He said Lebanese President Joseph Aoun “has not acted as an arbiter, nor as a unifying figure, but has become biased and divisive, which is incompatible with his role and with Lebanon’s strength”. The head of the Iran-backed group also accused Lebanese authorities of having “helped Israel instead of helping Lebanon’s sovereignty” by continuing with negotiations that he said had handed Israel “political gains”. PM Salam’s riposte Prime Minister Nawaf Salam hit back on X, saying “the greatest help to Israel was provided by those who unilaterally drew Lebanon into the adventures of futile wars… and granted it pretexts to attack our country”. “Those who unilaterally take the decision of war and try to continue to seize the state’s decision-making, and to tie Lebanon to foreign calculations and axes, ignoring the interests of their community and the Lebanese in general, are not fit to lecture on patriotism, not to mention on sovereignty,” Salam added. “Lebanon has no sovereignty except for the sole independent decision of the state with one army which extends its authority over all its territory,” Salam added. Hezbollah has repeatedly rejected the direct talks and refuses to surrender its weapons. Violence has decreased since the Lebanon-Israel deal, but Lebanon continues to report intermittent Israeli strikes, shelling and heavy demolitions in southern villages and towns. “Shouldn’t the systematic destruction of southern villages and towns… be reason for the political authorities to say, ‘We don’t want dialogue with the Israeli entity’”, Qassem said. He vowed “to make the utmost effort to provide the means for shelter, repairs and reconstruction”, cautioning however that this would require “patience”. Direct talks Meanwhile, Lebanon and Israel held a fresh round of US-sponsored talks in Rome on Tuesday, with Beirut seeking Israel’s phased withdrawal from the south. This week’s negotiations are the seventh round of Washington-mediated talks since the outbreak of the US-Iran war on Feb 28. On Monday, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani urged Lebanon and Israel to “continue in a constructive spirit, identifying shared solutions that will allow for the full implementation of the framework agreement”. After talks last month, Israel’s military withdrew from the outskirts of the village of Zawtar al Gharbiya, one of the first pilot zones. The Lebanese army deployed to the area and has allowed residents to inspect their homes and businesses. Published in Dawn, August 5th, 2026

Two gas utilities to become five. ISLAMABAD: The government is once again finalising plans to unbundle the country’s two gas utilities into five smaller companies — one transmission company and four provincial distribution firms — on the pattern of the more than 15 ex-Wapda generation, transmission and distribution companies. The proposed gas sector reforms, including the unbundling of Sui Northern Gas Pipelines Ltd (SNGPL) and Sui Southern Gas Company Ltd (SSGCL), were discussed on Tuesday at a meeting led by Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik on the government side and by World Bank Country Director for Pakistan, Bolormaa Amgaabazar, on the other. “The reform framework also proposes the restructuring and unbundling of the Sui companies by separating their transmission, distribution and energy businesses, while creating greater opportunities for private sector participation throughout the gas value chain,” an official statement said after the meeting. Informed sources said some major business groups were interested in the transmission business through privatisation. However, the distribution sector faced serious challenges due to issues such as transfer pricing, cross-subsidies, and uniform national gas prices despite varying levels of system losses — the highest in Balochistan, followed by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh, and Punjab. Govt plans splitting SNGPL, SSGCL into one transmission and four provincial distribution companies Independent consultant KPMG and the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) had previously opposed the proposed unbundling model on financial and technical viability grounds and suggested broader consultations, including with the provinces and private shareholders. The plan was eventually shelved in 2020. The sources said the Petroleum Division now wanted to fast-track the restructuring and unbundling process and secure the prime minister’s approval this month. “The meeting reviewed and endorsed the strategic direction of Pakistan’s gas sector reforms,” the statement said, adding that the minister directed officials to prepare the finalised roadmap for the prime minister’s approval by the end of August 2026. “Following the prime minister’s approval, the Petroleum Division will initiate phased implementation of the reform programme in consultation with all stakeholders to ensure a smooth and sustainable transition to a modern, competitive and financially viable gas sector,” it added. For this purpose, the Petroleum Division will seek the immediate appointment of a transaction adviser to work out the unbundling of SNGPL and SSGCL into five companies. The adviser’s cost would either be financed by the World Bank or shared equally by the two gas utilities and recovered through end-consumer tariffs. Interestingly, both companies and their shareholders oppose the proposed unbundling — effectively their dissolution — and are also unwilling to finance the process for obvious reasons. Under the plan, a National Gas Transmission Company (NGTC) would be carved out to take over the transmission systems and business of both gas utilities and operate as a common carrier for the existing and newly created gas distribution companies, similar to the National Transmission and Dispatch Company (NTDC) in the power sector, now renamed National Grid Company. The proposal envisages third-party access by private firms to the NGTC network. The transmission company would not itself engage in the sale or purchase of gas; instead, it would transport gas and charge wheeling fees to all suppliers and purchasers of locally produced gas or LNG. Some influential business groups with connections in policymaking circles are also said to be interested in acquiring a stake in the NGTC. The distribution networks of both utilities would then be divided into multiple gas distribution companies operating under unified principles within the jurisdictions of SNGPL and SSGCL. These smaller business units would be formed based on technical and economic criteria, including population, network density, gas demand, workload, supervision, and operational efficiency, to ensure their sustainability. The plan would also require a mechanism for weighted average sale price equalisation, or another suitable pricing mechanism, for gas sales. However, there is still a view within the Petroleum Division that the matter should be decided in consultation with all stakeholders and provincial governments, including approval from the Council of Common Interests (CCI), before appointing any consultant, since the terms of reference for the adviser would depend on the agreed mechanism. There is also opposition to splitting the two existing companies into five or more entities before the transaction adviser completes the advisory process, particularly regarding the feasibility of the proposed reforms. Nepal mourns ‘generation lost’ to Broad Peak avalanche. • Around 500 mourners, monks gather in Kathmandu • Funeral of missing Pakistani climber held in Hunza • Efforts continue to recover bodies amid bad weather KATHMANDU/GILGIT: Hund­­reds of Nepalis held a candlelight vigil on Tuesday honouring 10 climbers killed in an avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak, as rescuers battled treacherous conditions to recover the remaining bodies. Buddhist monks in maroon robes chanted prayers and around 500 mourners lit candles and incense in a square in the Nepali capital. World-renowned British-Nepali climber Nirmal Purja, 43, was among the victims along with six elite Nepali guides, killed in the avalanche in Gilgit-Baltistan on Thursday. “Nepal has lost a generation of accomplished mountaineers,” said Tul Singh Gurung, president of Nepal National Mountain Guide Association. The gathering observed a minute’s silence in their memory, in front of a banner with photographs of the 10 climbers. At the centre, candles were arranged in the shape of Nepal’s national flag, flickering in the dusk. “This is a big loss for our mountaineering sector,” said Man Raj Gurung, an international mountain guide. “I think it might take years for us to see such climbers again, because not everyone will be willing to take on such a risky job.” News of the avalanche has prompted tributes from across the climbing community and beyond. In 2019, Purja stunned the climbing fraternity by scaling the world’s 14 highest peaks in just over six months, shattering the previous record of seven years. His feat was later chronicled in a Netflix documentary, helping inspire a new generation of climbers and elevating Nepal’s profile in a sport long dominated by Western adventurers. Two years later, he was part of the historic all-Nepali team that completed the first winter ascent of K2, the world’s second-highest mountain and one of mountaineering’s most dangerous challenges. In his hometown in Ramnagar in southern Nepal, where his brother lives with his family, people have been coming to grieve and pay tribute around a framed photograph of Purja. Meanwhile, funeral prayers in absentia for Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi were offered in his hometown of Aliabad in Hunza on Monday, where hundreds of people paid tribute to the young mountaineer and offered condolences to his family after they announced his death. The body of Sohail Sakhi, who went missing along with nine other members of an expedition after an avalanche struck Broad Peak — the world’s 12th highest mountain in GB — has yet to be recovered despite an extensive search and rescue operation. Since the avalanche struck on July 30, the remains of eight climbers have been recovered, while the bodies of two others, including Sohail Sakhi and a Nepali Sherpa, are still missing. In a statement, Darwish Ali, the late climber’s uncle, said the family had made the painful decision “with profound sorrow after enduring days of hope, uncertainty and prayers”. A large number of people visited Sakhi’s home to offer condolences, expressing grief over the loss of the young climber and praying for his departed soul. Darwish Ali said Sohail’s mother had been admitted to a local hospital in Aliabad after suffering trauma and high blood pressure following the family’s announcement of his death. The four bodies recovered on Sunday were identified as those of Nirmal Purja, China’s Wang Zhong, Nepal’s Nima Sherpa and Kili Pemba Sherpa. However, they could not be shifted to the base camp due to bad weather. The remains of Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy of Oman, Pur Bahadur Gurung and Gyalu Sherpa of Nepal, and Sarah Mallory Geis of the United States were recovered on July 31 and Aug 1 and airlifted to Skardu. According to sources at the Broad Peak base camp, recovery efforts continued under extremely difficult terrain conditions on Monday. Heli­copter operations could not be carried out on Monday and Tuesday bec­ause of adverse weather. Sources said helicopter sling operations would be required to retrieve the bodies. Meanwhile, rescue teams continued searching for the bodies of Soh­ail Sakhi and the missing Nepali climber. Published in Dawn, August 5th, 2026

IHC suspends order for disclosure of cricketers’ salaries, perks. ISLAMABAD: The Isla­mabad High Court on Tuesday suspended a Pakistan Information Comm­ission (PIC) order that directed the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) to make public its annual budgets, audit reports, remuneration of national players, selection committee members, and expenditure on the T20 World Cup 2026. A single-member bench of Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar issued notices to respondents for September 22, 2026, while taking up a writ petition filed by the PCB through Advocate Kashif Ali Malik. The court stayed the operation of the PIC’s July 9 ruling until the next hearing. The PCB contended that the impugned order was passed in excess of jurisdiction and in violation of the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017. It argued that the Commission had failed to distinguish between information liable to proactive disclosure under Section 5 and information protected under statutory exemptions relating to personal privacy, confidential contractual arrangements, commercially sensitive data, and third-party interests. The PCB, which generates its revenues primarily through commercial activities rather than government funding, maintained that the information sought extended beyond institutional expenditure to personal financial details of identifiable individuals, without recognising the distinction between institutional transparency and private financial affairs. The board has faced persistent scrutiny over financial transparency. Since the appointment of Chairman Mohsin Naqvi in 2024, the PCB has discontinued the practice of posting detailed financial statements on its website, a departure from previous norms that had drawn criticism from transparency advocates and prompted the underlying information requests. Assistant Attorney Gen­eral Asif Khan Jadoon also appeared before the court. The court also allowed the PCB’s exemption application subject to all just and legal exceptions. The matter has been adjourned until September 22, 2026. Published in Dawn, August 5th, 2026

Rethinking governance in Pakistan. EVERY few years, Pakistan revisits the debate on creating new provinces. The interior minister’s recent proposal to establish smaller administrative units has again raised an important question. Yet the real issue is not how many provinces Pa­­kistan should have. It is whether government is close enough to serve its citizens effectively. Adm­inistrative boundaries matter only because they influence how quickly people receive education, healthcare, justice, infrastructure and disaster relief. If governance remains distant and unresponsive, merely redrawing maps won’t improve lives. With over 240 million people spread across nearly 796,000 square kilometres, Pakistan is one of the world’s largest federations. Its administrative challenges vary enormously — from the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan to the deserts of Thar and the vast expanse of Balochistan. A governance model suited to Lahore or Karachi cannot automatically meet the needs of Kech, Upper Kohistan or Astore. The real challenge is one of state capacity rather than geography alone. Pakistan’s history reflects repeated efforts to balance national unity with effective administration. At independence in 1947, West Pakistan comprised Punjab, Sindh, the North-West Frontier Province, the Chief Commissioner’s Province of Balochistan, princely states — including Kalat, Bahawalpur and Swat — and the Tribal Areas. The 1955 One Unit scheme attempted to centralise administration; instead, it deepened regional grievances. Its abolition in 1970 and the federal framework established by the 1973 Constitution reaffirmed the importance of provincial autonomy. More recently, the merger of Fata into KP demonstrated that Pakistan’s administrative structure can evolve when necessary. Yet demands for South Punjab, Hazara and Bahawalpur continue because many citizens still feel distant from provincial capitals. The case for smaller administrative units is fundamentally administrative rather than political. Punjab’s population exceeds that of many countries, while Balochistan covers almost 44 per cent of Pakistan’s territory but contains only a small share of its population. Administering such contrasting regions through similar institutional arrangements limits efficiency. Have power, resources and decision-making been devolved enough to serve citizens effectively? Governments perform best when decision-makers are close to the communities they serve. Greater administrative proximity improves supervision of schools, hospitals, roads and development projects while strengthening transparency and public accountability. The devastating floods of 2022 illustrated the value of capable local institutions. Where local administrative capacity was stronger, relief reached affected communities more quickly. At the same time, creating new provinces is neither simple nor inexpensive. Constitutional ame­n­­dments require broad political consensus, while new provinces need legislatures, secretariats, ju­­d­­icial institutions and sustainable financial res­o­u­­rces. Without careful planning, administrative re­­organisation risks creating additional bureaucracy without significantly improving governance. International experience offers useful lessons. India has repeatedly created new states — including Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Uttarakhand and Telangana — to improve governance in historically neglected regions. Although disputes over assets and water accompanied these reforms, smaller states enabled governments to focus more closely on local priorities. Bangladesh adopted a different approach. Rather than creating provinces, it strengthened districts, upazilas and union parishads. Improvements in rural healthcare, primary education and disaster management owe much to effective local administration. Indonesia embarked on one of the world’s largest decentralisation programmes after reforms in 1998, transferring substantial authority and financial resources to districts and municipalities. Nigeria, by contrast, demonstrates the risks of expanding administrative units without fiscal sustainability; while political representation improved, the country developed an expensive state structure heavily dependent on federal revenues. France provides yet another model, devolving significant powers to departments and municipalities without repeatedly altering regional boundaries. Despite their different political systems, these countries illustrate one common principle: successful administrative reform depends less on the number of administrative units than on whether authority, financial resources and accountability actually reach local institutions. Ironically, Pakistan already possesses the constitutional foundation for this approach. Article 140A requires provinces to establish elected local governments and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility to them. Yet successive governments have implemented this provision unevenly. Pakistan’s own experience supports stronger LG. The 2001 Local Government Plan transferred significant responsibilities for education, healthcare and local development to elected district governments. Although politically controversial, it demonstrated the benefits of bringing decision-making closer to citizens. After the 18th Amendment, provinces gained substantial autonomy from Islamabad, but meaningful decentralisation often stopped at the provincial level. Many districts and municipalities remained dependent on provincial governments for authority and funding. Thus, the debate over new provinces and LG should be seen as complementary rather than competing. Where there is broad public consensus, administrative necessity and economic viability, new provinces should remain a legitimate constitutional option. But such reforms must be guided by transparent criteria and accompanied by agreed arrangements for finance, water, civil services and transitional administration. At the same time, meaningful LG reform should begin immediately. Provinces should guarantee predictable financial transfers to elected LGs, devolve responsibility for primary education, basic healthcare, water supply, sanitation and local infrastructure, conduct regular local elections, and protect local institutions from arbitrary dissolution. Devolution without financial autonomy cannot succeed. For nearly eight decades, Pakistan has alternated between centralisation and decentralisation, often expecting structural changes alone to resolve governance failures. Experience at home and abroad suggests otherwise. Institutions matter more than boundaries. The purpose of administrative reform is not to redraw maps but to improve lives. When a child in Rajanpur, Tharpar­kar, Upper Kohistan, Kech, Astore or Neelum Valley enjoys the same access to education and healthcare as one in Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar, Quetta or Islamabad; when a mother in Dera Bugti can obtain timely medical care; and when citizens across Punjab, Sindh, KP, Balochistan, GB and Azad Kashmir experience responsive public institutions, Pakistan will know that administrative reform has achieved its purpose. A federation’s true strength is measured not by the number of provinces on its map, but by the confidence of its citizens that their government is never too distant to serve them. The writer is a retired inspector general of police and former DG FIA. Published in Dawn, August 5th, 2026

State of confusion. FROM the looks of it, America has no exit strategy to extricate itself from the disastrous war with Iran. US President Donald Trump has alternated between issuing bombastic threats to the Iranians, to claiming that peace was at hand, sometimes making a sharp U-turn within hours. This is not how responsible statecraft plays out. In the past, he had threatened to destroy Iranian civilisation, while more recently he said the US was ready to use “Military Terror … not seen since World War II” against the Islamic Republic. In his latest pronouncement, the US leader has given Iran a “last chance” to choose between a “deal [or] total surrender”. The five-month-old war has shown that the Iranians have mostly remained unfazed by Mr Trump’s threats. The chaos at the White House is understandable. Mr Trump jumped headfirst into the war on Feb 28 at Israel’s persuasion, without doing his homework. Perhaps if he had studied the mistakes his predecessors had made in Afghanistan, Iraq and Libya, he would have refrained from launching a new war. But the US leader is not known for deep reflection, not even on critical issues. There are reports — officially denied by Washington — that the US is running low on key munitions, while many of America’s top generals have warned their bosses that there are no longer many good military options available. As per one report, Centcom has solicited , via email, “new creative and unconventional ways to … punish Iran”, from defence experts. In plain speak, there is policy chaos in Washington. Moreover, there are reports that the Saudis have asked the US to give diplomacy with Iran another try. Riyadh realises that immense destruction will engulf the region should another round of hostilities break out. It is very difficult for leaders to admit they are wrong. But it is crucial for Mr Trump to realise that Operation ‘Epic Fury’ has been an epic failure. The US has achieved none of its objectives. Iran evidently retains its nuclear capabilities; it has pledged to continue supporting its regional armed allies; and its control over the Strait of Hormuz has only increased since the war began. In addition, the American and Israeli dream of regime change has completely backfired: the pragmatic old guard — assassinated by the US and Israel — has been replaced by an ideologically driven and much more hard-line new leadership. From this point on, the US should shun its violent rhetoric and approach the Iranians with respect. Pakistan, which Iran has identified as a key mediator, can press on with its efforts to revive the Islamabad MoU . If it decides to continue with more threats, Washington will only sink deeper into the Iran quagmire, as the hard-liners in the Islamic Republic’s establishment seem determined to fight on. Published in Dawn, August 5th, 2026

Unravelling order. IT is not so much what he said as who said it. We all know that the existing political system has failed to deliver, but that admission coming from the all-powerful interior minister raises many questions. Mohsin Naqvi is himself a product of a system whose legitimacy he is now questioning . His statement points to the unravelling of the hybrid arrangement. What he said cannot be dismissed as merely his personal views, given his perceived association with the powers that be. Speaking at the Pakistan Economic Summit last week, the interior minister said the current system of governance had “collapsed” and that it was fundamentally incapable of resolving the country’s problems. He stressed the need for structural reform to address Pakistan’s mounting challenges. No one can disagree with Naqvi’s assertion. But his suggestion of creating new administrative units as a means of improving governance and his thinly veiled criticism of his own government’s policies have laid bare the fault lines within the hybrid political structure established after the controversial 2024 elections. Naqvi’s statement was later tacitly endorsed by the military spokesman, who also urged political parties to consider an administrative reset to improve governance, arguing that the country’s security and stability depended on adapting its governance structure to the requirements of modern times and a growing population. The statement has also generated speculation about the Shehbaz Sharif government’s survival less than halfway through its term. Given the historically brief tenures of civilian governments, such uncertainty is deeply rooted. The interior minister’s remarks have jolted the ruling coalition, with some federal ministers questioning Naqvi’s own credentials. Yet while chastising him, they understand that he is not answerable even to the cabinet or the prime minister. The interior minister should focus on security rather than administrative reorganisation. In the words of Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, Naqvi is a “powerhouse” who is not answerable to anyone. A man for all seasons, as he is referred to by some, Naqvi deals with everything from cricket to security and even ventures into foreign policy. He seldom attends cabinet meetings or appears in parliament. He is not a member of any political party, yet is arguably the most powerful person in the government after the prime minister. Most analysts agree that he draws his power from close ties with the establishment. Naqvi’s journey from media professional to one of the most powerful political positions in the country began when he was appointed caretaker chief minister of Punjab, the country’s most powerful province, in 2023. He joined the federal cabinet after the 2024 elections. Recently, he was also involved in Pakistan’s mediation efforts during the US-Iran war. His meteoric rise defines where the balance of power lies. His indictment of the government was not just a spontaneous outburst; it lays out a plan for a political and administrative reset. The statements of the interior minister and military spokesman must be read together to make sense of what appears to be in store. The ‘restructuring’ plan is likely to intensify the existing chaos rather than bring political stability. While both officials pointed to the absence of governance, the real cause behind this state of affairs wasn’t mentioned. It is easy to blame the politicians for all the problems, but there is no mention of other obvious factors. Naqvi regretted that the ‘failed system’ had been dragged on for seven decades. He is absolutely right, but he failed to mention the dominant influence of the security apparatus for much of the country’s history. The decline of the present hybrid, and increasingly autocratic, system was long foretold. A mere change of face and creation of new administrative units will not solve the state’s problems. Many view the statements as an attempt to redirect public attention from the real issues and tighten control. More important than the creation of new provinces is the devolution of administrative power to the local level and the restoration of democratic rights. Any imposed plan for the creation of new provinces or administrative units would further destabilise the country. While the current political discourse has been revolving around the two statements and speculation about impending changes, the country faces an existential internal security threat, with terrorism now spreading despite the establishment’s claim that the situation is under control. The latest terrorist attack in Swat , which killed several policemen, is a grim reminder that terrorism has returned to the district after years of calm. Notwithstanding the claim of successful intelligence-based operations, there seems to be a complete breakdown of law and order in KP, with an increasing number of terrorist attacks targeting an underequipped police force, whose personnel are sitting ducks in the face of sophisticatedly armed militants. Some protests by police have also been reported from the troubled districts over being left alone to fight the better-armed terrorists. Meanwhile, the situation in Balochistan and Azad Kashmir has worsened, with the state relying entirely on kinetic options to deal with a largely political problem. The ongoing elections in AJK have been marred by reports of violence and allegations of electoral manipulation. No blackout of the news can change the reality on the ground. Would it not be better for the interior minister to focus on his main job of ensuring security, rather than trying to create more administrative units? The latest poll controversy has unravelled the ruling coalition and exposed the hypocrisy of the component parties. The PML-N and the PPP are now at daggers drawn, accusing each other of being undemocratic. Although it is a beneficiary of the system itself, the PPP is now accusing the PML-N of being a product of Form 47 — a fact it had previously refused to accept. The writer is an author and journalist. zhussain100@yahoo.com X: @hidhussain Published in Dawn, August 5th, 2026

CJP Afridi promises women facilitation centres in courts nationwide. KARACHI: Chief Justice of Pakistan (CJP) Yahya Afridi on Tuesday said that women facilitation centres will be established in courts across the country to provide a safe, dignified, accessible and supportive environment for female litigants. He also stated that the proposed facilitation centres will include dedicated reception areas, waiting areas, separate entrances, washrooms, meeting rooms, alternative dispute resolution facilities, legal advisory services, psychosocial support services, and other essential support facilities designed to facilitate women litigants and visitors. The CJP was speaking to the women representatives of the Sindh High Court Bar Association and the Karachi Bar Association during a meeting held at the Supreme Court Karachi Registry. Sindh High Court Chief Justice Zafar Ahmed Rajput as well as the presidents and secretaries of both bars were also present. CJP Afridi shared his vision for strengthening women-friendly judicial infrastructure and further said that pursuant to a decision of the National Judicial (Policy Making) Committee, 2026-27 has been designated as the year of priority for women litigants’ facilitation, under which women facilitation centres will be established in courts across Pakistan. He also stated that the initiative aims to provide a safe, dignified, accessible and supportive environment for women seeking justice, ensuring their privacy, security, comfort and ease of access to judicial services. He added that such centres will have essential support facilities designed to facilitate women litigants and visitors. The CJP further informed the participants that under the auspices of the Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan, the Institute of Architects Pakistan had conducted a nationwide design competition for such facilitation centres and the top three designs have been selected and will be shared with all high courts as model designs to facilitate the establishment of facilitation centres across the country. According to a statement issued by the SC, the women representatives of both bars appreciated the initiative and also highlighted various issues concerning women’s access to justice and the legal profession. The CJP assured them that their concerns would be addressed on a priority basis. Published in Dawn, August 5th, 2026

The case for smaller administrative units in the age of AI. Let us be honest about something Pakistan’s governance discourse rarely says plainly: political parties do not want local governments to work. This is not a failure of will or capacity. It is a deliberate choice, repeated by every party in every province across every cycle of government, regardless of ideology, coalition or electoral mandate. Local bodies are constituted late, funded poorly, stripped of administrative authority and dissolved early. The pattern is too consistent, too cross-partisan and too durable to be accidental. It is policy by other means. A rival power centre The reason is straightforward. A functioning local government is a rival power centre. It has an electoral base, a budget, a staff and a mandate to deliver services that citizens can see and touch. It can build a political constituency independent of the provincial party machine. For parties whose power rests on controlling the distribution of roads, postings, contracts and patronage from the provincial capital, that is an existential threat not to the state but to them. So they keep the tier alive enough to satisfy constitutional requirements and dead enough to pose no challenge. The local body hence becomes a holding cell for lower-tier party workers, not a governing institution. Waiting for parties to change this calculus is not a strategy. No party in power has ever voluntarily strengthened a tier of government that could constrain it. The few periods of active local government in Pakistan’s history: the 1960s Basic Democracies, the 2001 devolution under Musharraf and the post-18th Amendment councils were all driven by either military governments with no electoral stakes or by court orders that were subsequently ignored by political parties. Democratic parties have never, left to themselves, built strong local governments. Expecting them to do so now is to misread the incentive structure entirely. Meanwhile, the citizen’s need for governance does not wait. Sewage backs up. Schools sit without teachers. Basic registrations, certificates, and permits require travel to a city three hours away. Climate shocks, floods, heat waves and droughts demand local response capacity that no provincial capital can provide at speed. The gap between what people need and what the state delivers grows wider each year and the existing institutional architecture with four massive provinces, a thin federal tier and a local layer that exists mostly on paper cannot close it. The fix If parties will not allow local governments to function, the logic points toward a different structural fix; smaller administrative units. Not smaller local bodies within existing provinces, but the provinces themselves reconfigured or supplemented by administrative divisions drawn on rational, service-delivery grounds. Units small enough that a single administration can actually sense and respond to local conditions. Units where the district health officer knows the district and where the education planner is not managing the scale of a mid-sized European country from a single office building. The critical question is the basis on which these units are drawn. Ethnicity and language are the obvious political demands, but they are the wrong answer. Ethnic administrative boundaries encode group competition into the map permanently. Every resource allocation becomes a proxy for ethnic power. Every appointment is a signal about whose territory this is. Countries that draw administrative lines on ethnic logic spend their governance energy managing the boundary itself rather than delivering services within it. Pakistan, with its layered ethnic, linguistic, sectarian and tribal identities — many of which overlap, shift and are internally contested — cannot afford administrative units that calcify those identities into state structures. The alternative is ruthlessly administrative logic: population thresholds, geographic coherence, economic connectivity, river basin and infrastructure alignment and service delivery catchment areas. A unit that can support a tertiary hospital, a polytechnic institute, a land records office and a local court without borrowing capacity from a neighbouring unit. Boundaries drawn by asking what geography enables efficient governance, not by asking which group lives here. This is not ethnicity-blind; a sensible administration accounts for linguistic diversity in staffing and communication but it refuses to make ethnicity the organising principle of the state’s internal architecture. The tools are available This is where the twenty-first century offers Pakistan something it did not have in earlier rounds of administrative reform: the tools to actually run small units efficiently. Artificial intelligence, digital service delivery and real-time data platforms are collapsing the administrative cost of small-scale governance. A local administration no longer needs to physically house every function. AI-powered triage systems can route citizen complaints, allocate maintenance crews and flag anomalies in service delivery faster and more accurately than a provincial bureaucracy managing 10 million people from a single dashboard. Land records, business registrations, birth and death certificates and public grievance systems can all run on shared digital infrastructure, with the local unit as a point of contact rather than the processor. In an AI-assisted governance model, the case for large administrative units historically justified by economies of scale in bureaucratic capacity largely disappears. What you need at scale is a shared technology layer, shared standards and interoperable data systems. What you need locally is a small, elected or appointed administration with genuine authority, a budget tied to local revenue and population and accountability to the people who live there. The AI layer handles the complexity that used to require size. The local layer handles the judgment, the presence and the trust. Several countries are already moving in this direction. Estonia’s entire public administration operates at a scale: 1.3 million people that is comparable to a mid-sized Pakistani district and its digital governance stack is the backbone of service delivery rather than a supplement to bureaucracy. Rwanda reorganised its districts in 2006 on service-delivery logic, not ethnic logic after the catastrophic lesson of what ethnic administrative boundaries produce. South Korea’s smart city initiatives embed real-time sensing and AI-driven resource allocation at the municipal level. The direction is consistent: governance is becoming more local, more data-driven and less dependent on administrative mass. Pakistan’s current map is a colonial inheritance optimised for revenue extraction and security control, not for citizen service. The four-province structure, including Gilgit Baltistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir, whatever its historical justification, was never designed around the question of what unit of government could best respond to a family that needs a functioning school, a clean water connection and a place to file a legal complaint. Answering that question now with the tools available in 2026 points toward smaller units, administrative boundaries and a digital backbone that gives those units the capacity that size used to provide. The parties will resist. They always do. But the argument for smaller, rationally drawn administrative units does not require party consent; it requires a constitutional conversation about what the state is for. Pakistan’s citizens have been patient with an architecture that was never built for them. The AI era doesn’t just make better governance possible. It makes the old excuses for not delivering it obsolete.

Pakistan close on series-levelling win against West Indies. Pakistan’s spinners put their team on course for a series-levelling victory as the West Indies stumbled to 103 for six — a lead of just 60 runs — on an eventful third day of the second and final Test in Trinidad on Tuesday. Abdullah Shafique’s unbeaten 160 ensured the visitors did not completely squander an excellent overnight platform in eventually getting to a first-innings total of 387. Sajid Khan then made his second meaningful contribution of the day in taking four second-innings wickets, while Ali Usman claimed two, including home captain Roston Chase caught-and-bowled off the final ball of the day. First-innings top-scorer Justin Greaves will carry the fight for the West Indies into the fourth morning with uncertainty over the availability to bat of regular opener Brandon King. On a deteriorating pitch offering sharp turn and variable bounce, West Indies left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican was as much in his element as 18 months earlier against these same opponents in Multan. Here, his haul of six for 112, including three wickets in four balls to wrap up the Pakistan innings on the stroke of tea, would have been a portent of things to come. Yet having started the day in the comfortable position of 266 for two and within sight of the West Indies first-innings total of 344, it took an error of judgement from captain Babar Azam to trigger a gradual slide as the visitors’ last eight wickets fell for 106 runs. Having put the West Indies bowlers to the sword with delightful, confident strokeplay on the second afternoon, Babar was a picture of strokeless paralysis at the start of the day, as if the prospect of a first Test century in almost four years had gotten the better of him. He managed to eke out a couple of runs to add to his overnight 86 before taking off for a non-existent single and, sent back by Shafique, dived desperately but in vain as the direct hit at the striker’s end by King from point found Babar short of his ground. West Indian delight at Babar’s dismissal was transformed to concern over the welfare of King, who remained prone on the outfield after effecting the dismissal. After several minutes of assessment of his situation, he was stretchered off with what was later diagnosed to be back spasms. That unexpected breakthrough triggered a mini-slide as three wickets fell for five runs, fast bowler Shamar Joseph and Warrican claiming a wicket each. Khan offered a measure of stability with Shafique, the pair putting on 59 for the seventh wicket before another pacer, Jayden Seales, removed the lower-order batsman for 30. With the door open to a vulnerable tail, Warrican wasted no time in wrapping up the innings, taking three wickets in four balls with Shafique stranded at the non-striker’s end and leaving Pakistan to rue opportunities missed to earn a much more significant lead. ‘Excellent’ Warrican-Shafique’s innings occupied more than seven-and-a-half hours during which he faced 323 deliveries, striking 15 fours and three sixes. “Jomel was really excellent for us today, staying at the stumps and finishing off the innings well,” said West Indies bowling coach Ravi Rampaul. “At this stage though, and given the way the pitch is playing, if we can somehow push the lead to 150 we would have a chance.” Khan was at his most rampant in the final session, accounting for Tagenarine Chanderpaul and Amir Jangoo swiftly before adding Shai Hope and nightwatchman Seales to his list of victims. Chase surveyed the carnage from the other end only to succumb to the constant pressure himself, the reaction of the home skipper to his demise almost a mirror of Babar’s disconsolate trek to the pavilion more than seven hours earlier. Usman also posed a constant threat, the left-arm spinner having earlier removed Kavem Hodge, whose 34 is the top score so far in an innings in danger of going into complete freefall.

Trump warns Iran to open Strait of Hormuz or get 'hit very hard'. United States President Donald Trump said a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could come as soon as Wednesday but warned Iran it would get “hit very hard” if negotiations fell through. Transit of the waterway, a key conduit for global oil and gas supplies, has been a sticking point in talks and led to renewed fighting following an April ceasefire. Iran has tightened its grip on Hormuz and wants to control the strait and charge tolls — powers it did not exercise before the war began on February 28. Trump said on Tuesday a deal with Iran to reopen Hormuz could happen “tomorrow or the next day,” telling reporters in California that negotiators “had a very good day”. Earlier, he struck a more threatening tone. “The strait is going to be open very soon, or they’re going to get hit very hard — and then the strait’s going to be open,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News. “All you can do is fight your way out.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC earlier “there is a chance we may have a deal” by Wednesday or Thursday. Underlining the volatile situation, one crew member was listed missing Tuesday on a merchant ship hit by a projectile in Hormuz, while an Indian ship in the Red Sea sank following an unattributed attack. In what has become a regular pattern, Trump last week threatened to hit Iran “very hard”, potentially with attacks against civilian infrastructure, only to pull back, hinting a deal was near. Iran’s foreign ministry has denied negotiations with Washington, even as Trump insisted they were happening. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that the US was involved in negotiations between Oman and Iran on increasing traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. News outlet Axios reported on Tuesday that the US, Iran and Oman were nearing an interim deal to reopen the strait, which Washington was hoping to announce on Wednesday. Axios , citing unnamed regional officials and a US official, said the deal on the table would be a 60-day arrangement for safe passage in the strait between Iran and Oman. Deal or surrender Qatar, which has been mediating negotiations, said that diplomatic efforts were ongoing but that no direct Iran-US talks were planned. Its leader, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani, spoke with Trump by phone on Tuesday, with Doha saying they discussed “efforts to de-escalate tensions.” Trump had previously said he expected to know by Tuesday how the talks were going, “one way or the other”, but insisted “it’s not very complex”. Washington’s diplomatic goals include reopening Hormuz and the denuclearisation of Iran, which Trump accepted could “take a little while.” The president previously called Tehran “ duplicitous ” for saying it was not negotiating, adding that a US counter-blockade of Iranian ports would remain “unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished”. More than five months into a war that has cost Washington billions of dollars, Iran remains able to fire missiles and drones at US and allied targets in the region, as well as at commercial shipping. Early on Tuesday, Britain’s maritime security agency UKMTO said an unnamed cargo vessel had been struck by an “unknown projectile” in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman. Iran continues to impose an effective blockade on the strait and insists ships coordinate crossings with it. Red Sea attack The disruptions in Hormuz have only placed greater importance on shipping lanes through the Red Sea, where Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu has enabled it to keep up shipments to global markets by circumventing Hormuz entirely. But since the Houthis announced their blockade, they have claimed attacks on multiple ships they say are in violation. On Tuesday, the Indian ship MSV Faize Noore Oliya sank in the Red Sea off Yemen following an unattributed attack, with all of its crew rescued.
